intro: August 2026 reveals a venture market in bifurcation: AI infrastructure and frontier models command 87.5% of U.S. venture capital while commanding only 62% of unicorn value through two companies, creating extreme concentration risk alongside structural challenges in founder retention, manufacturing bottlenecks, and geopolitical friction. Simultaneously, a broader pattern emerges of capital flowing toward defensible, boring infrastructure—from semiconductors to batteries to insurance defense law—as investors flee from software-only plays facing repricing pressures and recognize that AI's real bottlenecks are physical, not algorithmic.

themes.name: VC & Deal Flow
themes.synthesis:
The venture market has become a tale of extreme winner concentration masquerading as broad-based growth. OpenAI and Anthropic captured over half of the $407 billion in H1 2026 AI funding, yet represent only the 11th and 15th ranked companies on PitchBook's Business Quality framework—a damning signal that venture valuations have decoupled entirely from operational efficiency or unit economics. The median 2021-vintage VC fund has posted a 0.05x DPI, the worst on record, while four companies account for 93.5% of 2026 exit value. This is not a healthy market rewarding diverse innovation; it is a bubble concentrated in two frontier model providers and a handful of AI infrastructure bets, with the median founder experience resembling the dot-com era more than the venture comeback narrative.

A critical divergence has emerged between capital concentration and actual deal selectivity. While the venture market posted 9,366 deals worth $443.8 billion through August 2026, this represents a collapse from 8,290 deals in all of 2025—investors are deploying more capital but backing fewer companies. The culprit: federal tightening and AI enthusiasm have created a bifurcated market where Series D+ AI companies command 6.6x median valuation step-ups versus only 1.6x for non-AI peers. Secondary market data reveals the severity: AI startups funded recently trade at 0-5% discounts while 2021-2022 vintage companies face 54-59% discounts. This is not a rising tide. It is capital flowing from a drowning cohort directly into frontier AI while traditional tech businesses implode. The investment implication is stark: diversified VC returns have rebounded sharply in recent quarters, finally reversing four years of PE dominance, but this rebound is entirely driven by mega-winners, not broad-based portfolio performance. For institutional LPs, this signals both opportunity—capital efficiency and execution matter more than hype—and existential risk—most VC funds are underwater with negative net cash flows of $202 billion since 2022, starving emerging managers and accelerating concentration into mega-funds that can overprice deals.

The secondary layer of venture deal flow reveals the true source of future returns: manufacturing bottlenecks and vertical infrastructure. Defense tech funding surged 30-fold to $665 million in Q2 2026 driven by Pentagon demand for missile production, but actual manufacturing constraints in motors, explosives, and precision components create execution risk that capital alone cannot solve. Similarly, semiconductor funding hit $14.1 billion in H1 2026 on track to exceed 2025 by 50%, as investors recognize that defensibility in AI infrastructure lies not in software superiority but in supply constraints that won't ease until 2027 at earliest. Code Metal's $80 million Pentagon contract secured in under 12 months—an unusual acceleration for defense contracting—signals that the Pentagon is prepared to deploy capital at venture scale with compressed timelines, creating a new arbitrage opportunity for VC-backed companies willing to navigate compliance. The deeper insight: founders and investors who understand manufacturing, supply chains, and regulatory requirements will command premium valuations over consumer product founders chasing TAM expansion. Geographic arbitrage is simultaneously real. Washington DC VCs are achieving 11.7x MOIC versus 3.74x in the Bay Area and 3.18x in New York, driven by undersaturated founder networks and corporate headquarters hungry for local talent. Secondary cities represent a genuine return opportunity not because of superior deal quality but because of reduced competition and founder scarcity value.

themes.name: Enterprise Software & Agentic AI
themes.synthesis:
The enterprise software sector has entered a bifurcated repricing that will reshape venture returns for the remainder of this decade. Airtable's sale to Bending Spoons for $1.29 billion—an 81% discount to its $11 billion 2021 valuation—is not an isolated fire sale but a template for how $1+ billion venture-backed SaaS companies are being rationalized at ruinous prices. The broader pattern is unmistakable: Workday faces a potential $51 billion take-private by Silver Lake signaling confidence that large, embedded enterprise software platforms remain defensible against AI disruption, yet DoubleVerify was acquired for $13.60 per share, down from a $27 IPO and $43.52 peak, representing a systematic compression of software valuations despite headline growth. The 2021 vintage of late-stage SaaS companies will be remembered not as venture wins but as venture destruction of capital. Investors should expect a second correction phase in Q2 2026, where public markets demand proof of AI monetization before restoring valuations to pre-February levels.

The investment thesis has fundamentally shifted from horizontal SaaS to agentic AI with ERP-like characteristics, yet this shift creates a perilous timing problem for investors. PitchBook's analysis argues that agentic AI is evolving from a software category into organizational infrastructure with winner-take-most dynamics similar to ERP rather than SaaS, where better products quickly displace incumbents. This means early movers who establish vertical dominance and information advantages now will create defensible competitive positions that close in approximately one year. Yet the venture market has only begun pricing this dynamic—companies like HappyRobot achieved 5x revenue growth and 150%+ net dollar retention in enterprise automation, validating exceptional product-market fit in vertically-focused AI agents, but enterprise customers are expanding contracts 5-10x year-over-year precisely because they perceive no alternative solutions. The risk is timing: investors optimizing for near-term revenue multiples are using the wrong evaluation framework. The scorecard should emphasize market positioning, vertical penetration depth, and switching cost creation rather than traditional SaaS metrics like growth rates and margins. For PE investors, the Workday situation signals that large software platforms embedded in mission-critical workflows will command premium take-private valuations despite AI pressure, but only if they retain operational excellence and customer stickiness. The traditional PE playbook of multiple expansion is dead—the 2013-2018 era saw 58% of F&B buyout returns derive from multiple expansion versus only 16% in recent deals, signaling that PE must now focus relentlessly on revenue growth and operational improvement to generate returns.

The emerging competitive threat from AI models and specialized vertical players is eroding the defensibility of traditional enterprise software vendors. DeepMind's organizational turmoil—with CEO Demis Hassabis stepping down to chairperson and chief scientist Jeff Dean departing to launch Discovery Loop for automated scientific experimentation—signals that Google's control over frontier AI development is fracturing, with top talent fleeing to better-capitalized and more autonomous competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic. This brain drain compounds Google's technical setbacks: its latest models have fallen behind rivals on intelligence benchmarks and suffered repeated delays, marking a sharp reversal from its market-leading position. Similarly, the exodus of Lilian Weng from OpenAI signals that even inside the companies deemed indestructible, founder retention is collapsing as researcher-focused cultures, low barriers to entry, and secondary liquidity opportunities reduce long-term commitment incentives. For enterprise software investors, the implication is that frontier AI providers are cannibalizing enterprise workflows faster than traditional vendors can adapt. The investment question is whether pure-play agentic AI vertical vendors (like HappyRobot in supply chain negotiations) will remain independent winners or become acquisition targets for larger platforms seeking to vertically integrate before customers migrate entirely to AI-native solutions.

themes.name: AI Infrastructure & Semiconductors
themes.synthesis:
AI infrastructure has become the defining investment thesis of 2026, yet it masks a fundamental tension between capital availability and physical bottlenecks that will constrain returns for years. Semiconductor funding reached $14.1 billion in H1 2026, already tracking to exceed 2025 by nearly 50%, as investors increasingly view hardware as the critical bottleneck in AI's infrastructure buildout. Nvidia is raising $500 billion for AI infrastructure financing through GPU securitizations with major asset managers, spreading risk across insurance companies, pension funds, and sovereign wealth funds—a structure that allows institutional capital to deploy across different vehicles and suggests this template could become permanent across mega-scale infrastructure financing. Yet the announcement masks a critical vulnerability: Wall Street is betting heavily on sustained AI compute demand with limited hedges against disruptive scenarios. Investors should scrutinize whether Nvidia's 25% residual-value support mechanism adequately protects against efficiency improvements, policy constraints, or quantum computing disruption. The securitization structure itself signals both institutional confidence and systemic fragility—spreading risk across the financial system means a collapse in AI data center demand could cascade through insurance reserves and pension fund allocations rather than remain concentrated in tech sector losses.

The physical constraints on AI infrastructure are becoming the binding constraints on venture returns, with data center power demand, grid access, and water scarcity replacing semiconductor availability as the critical bottleneck. OpenAI is leasing a massive data center in Pike County, Ohio that will consume 10 gigawatts of electricity, requiring a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant to be built on federal land and financed by the Japanese government—a structure that signals AI companies are driving demand for mega-scale natural gas generation facilities, with Amazon and other developers planning similarly enormous gas plants in Texas. Georgia's Public Service Commission signaled rejection of OpenAI's $20 billion data center electricity supply contract, reflecting growing political resistance to AI infrastructure projects despite competing state incentives. Texas Governor Greg Abbott announced a freeze on new data center grid connections pending regulatory audit, joining New York Governor Kathy Hochul in slowing AI data center development ahead of elections. This regulatory friction is material: 530+ municipalities across the U.S. are now implementing local restrictions on data center development, forcing capital reallocation toward pre-approved facilities. The investment implication is that AI infrastructure investors must now price in permitting delays, political opposition, and regulatory uncertainty as material risk factors. Companies solving grid access bottlenecks—whether through demand flexibility, alternative power sources, or regulatory expertise—will command premium valuations not because they are more innovative but because they solve the binding constraint preventing capital deployment.

The geopolitical dimension of AI infrastructure is reshaping capital allocation patterns and creating new competitive vectors. Anthropic announced plans to acquire Decart, a world models and chip optimization software developer, for approximately $6 billion, positioning the AI company to potentially design its own chips and reduce compute costs ahead of its autumn IPO. SpaceX is pivoting aggressively toward AI infrastructure rental through its xAI subsidiary, with AI capex consuming 82.7% of total capital expenditures in 2026 at $23.5 billion, even as the Grok chatbot struggles in consumer and enterprise markets. The company is demonstrating profitability signs with xAI's adjusted EBITDA swinging from a $609 million Q1 loss to a $1.1 billion Q2 gain, suggesting either exceptional confidence in ROI potential or aggressive market timing concerns. Stripe's over $7 billion acquisition of OpenRouter signals that non-traditional tech companies are capturing disproportionate value by positioning themselves as neutral intermediaries between model developers and users. These moves collectively signal a shift in how AI infrastructure value is being captured: vertical integration into chip design, compute optimization, and payment infrastructure is becoming more valuable than pure-play model development. For investors, this suggests that the next phase of AI infrastructure returns will flow not to companies building better models but to those controlling the layers of the stack that remain scarce and defensible—chips, power, interconnect, and payment rails.

themes.name: Climate & Energy
themes.synthesis:
The climate and energy sector is experiencing a fundamental collision between stated climate commitments and actual capital allocation toward fossil fuel infrastructure, creating a bifurcated market where renewable energy investors face regulatory headwinds while fossil fuel upside accelerates. OpenAI's $20 billion Georgia data center faced regulatory delays as the state's Public Service Commission signaled rejection of the electricity supply contract, yet Amazon has been identified as the developer behind GW Ranch, a 7.7-gigawatt natural gas plant in Texas designed to power a data center campus. Tesla is advancing a $10 billion solar manufacturing facility in Texas as part of Musk's ambitious 100-gigawatt solar capacity expansion plan, yet simultaneously faces fierce Chinese competition and the expiration of U.S. federal solar tax credits. The Trump administration cancelled three federal transmission corridors designed to expedite grid expansion, citing concerns over costs, yet spent nearly $4 billion to cancel offshore wind projects that were already financially unviable. The pattern is unmistakable: tech companies including Microsoft, Google, and Meta are openly investing in natural gas infrastructure at scale, signaling that AI compute demands are driving a near-term return to fossil fuels rather than renewable energy, contradicting net-zero commitments and creating valuation disconnect risks for climate-focused funds.

The energy sector is simultaneously experiencing record profit margins from geopolitical supply shocks while facing political vulnerability from windfall tax proposals, creating a volatile macroeconomic environment for energy infrastructure investments. Chevron and Exxon posted record profits in Q2 2026 following supply shocks from Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz closure, with Chevron achieving its best quarterly results ever, yet President Trump publicly criticized both companies for "making too much money" and called for price cuts, reviving discussions about windfall profits taxes. U.S. natural gas production hit record levels at 122.5 billion cubic feet per day, driven by expanded drilling in the Permian and Haynesville regions, while Mitsubishi Heavy Industries' gas turbine backlog nearly doubled to 35 gigawatts by mid-2026, signaling sustained demand for natural gas infrastructure. The electric vehicle sector is simultaneously surging with unprecedented momentum—clean energy and transportation investment reached over $75 billion in Q2 2026, the second-largest quarter since 2018, driven primarily by consumer adoption of EVs and residential batteries hitting an all-time high of $11 billion in quarterly sales. Yet Ford's launch of the Fathom at $28,000 signals that mass-market EV competitiveness is finally arriving, potentially unlocking vehicle adoption at scale. The investment implication is that energy investors must now navigate a paradoxical market: fossil fuel margins are compressing despite near-term supply scarcity due to windfall tax risk, while renewable energy faces political headwinds but benefits from structural demand growth (EVs, grid storage, residential batteries) independent of policy incentives.

Water scarcity is emerging as a material constraint on AI infrastructure and data center siting, creating both risk and opportunity for investors in resilience and alternative cooling technologies. Tropical Storm Lala knocked out power to 200,000 homes across Hawaii's Big Island, exposing infrastructure vulnerabilities in a region rarely hit by direct storms, while the U.S. recorded its hottest month in 130+ years in July 2026 with Lake Mead hitting record lows amid severe western drought conditions. Data center community backlash is reshaping energy strategy: Corpus Christi, Texas faces potential water shortages, forcing the data center industry to shift from treating environmental concerns as communications issues to embedding water solutions into site selection. Arbor Energy is commercializing innovative modular turbines with oxy-combustion technology that generate water as a byproduct, representing a scalable alternative to traditional liquid cooling. An intense El Niño event is unfolding with sea surface temperatures 2.6 degrees Celsius above normal, making it the third strongest on record, expected to cost the global economy over $3 trillion and serve as a preview of normal climate conditions by the 2030s. This creates both existential risk and opportunity: water scarcity is becoming a material site selection constraint for data center development, creating first-mover advantage for companies with proven generation or recycling technologies. Grid-scale battery storage is the fastest-growing segment of U.S. energy infrastructure with 70% annual growth, and utilities are now using aggressive contractual terms (25-year 90% demand commitments) to secure long-term revenue from data center operators, shifting infrastructure costs to existing ratepayers. The investment implication is that climate adaptation infrastructure—from water generation to grid resilience to wildfire suppression—will attract substantial capital as communities recognize existential vulnerability, with winners being companies that solve material scarcity problems rather than incremental efficiency improvements.

themes.name: European VC & Fintech
themes.synthesis:
European venture capital is experiencing relative strength during a period of U.S. market contraction, with PE deal activity growing 6.9% in Q2 2026 despite ECB interest rate hikes while U.S. PE deal value fell 37.5%, signaling a structural divergence favoring European markets. The UK accounted for 30% of European PE deal value, its highest share since 2019, while mega-exits represented a decade-high 65.8% of total exit value. This geographic rotation is not driven by favorable financing conditions but by structural factors—market fragmentation and genuine alpha opportunities—indicating this trend may sustain through future rate cycles. Meanwhile, European tech leadership including Brevo founder Armand Thiberge is mobilizing for coordinated public investment in frontier AI models to compete with U.S.-China dominance, signaling that private VC capital alone is insufficient and that industrial policy investment vehicles may become the primary capital source for European AI competitiveness. Tomorrowland's launch of Lab of Tomorrow in Belgium—Europe's first accelerator dedicated to entertainment tech—positions Flanders as a potential secondary tech hub focused on vertical innovation, suggesting geographic diversification opportunities away from traditional VC clusters and potential government support for sector-specific infrastructure development.

Fintech regulation is hardening around banking charters and third-party risk management, creating both compliance burden and consolidation opportunity as the industry transitions from startup innovation to infrastructure standardization. Coastal Community Bank reported a $42 million loss in Q2 2024 primarily driven by losses from fintech partner LendingPoint, highlighting the risks banks face when partnering with consumer lending platforms and signaling that bank-fintech relationships are shifting from cooperative to adversarial as credit quality deteriorates. The OCC's rejection of bunq's federal charter application signals stricter capital and compliance standards for crypto-adjacent applicants, while the FDIC and major banking/fintech industry groups are collaboratively developing standards for third-party risk management, indicating a shift toward collaborative standard-setting rather than adversarial regulation. Lineage, a former Tennessee community bank that grew assets 790% in two years through fintech partnerships with Synapse, is now facing regulatory enforcement action, validating earlier warnings that fintech-dependent bank growth models create hidden concentration risk when middleware partners fail. The investment implication is that fintech infrastructure providers like Increase (moving upstream into banking operations) will face consolidation pressure as middleware becomes vertically integrated, while pure-play service providers face margin compression. Federal Reserve master account access has become a competitive bottleneck and headline risk, suggesting that direct central bank connectivity is now a critical differentiator for fintech viability rather than a commodity service.

themes.name: Deep Tech & Defense
themes.synthesis:
Defense tech funding is experiencing unprecedented acceleration, with capital surging 30-fold to $665 million in Q2 2026 driven by Pentagon demand for missile production, yet actual manufacturing constraints in motors, explosives, and precision components create execution risk that capital alone cannot solve. Code Metal's $80 million Pentagon contract secured in under 12 months—achieved through Salesforce Ventures backing and the Other Transaction Authority—signals that the Pentagon is prepared to deploy capital at venture scale with dramatically compressed timelines, creating a new arbitrage opportunity for VC-backed companies willing to navigate defense compliance requirements. Cambridge Aerospace, a British air defense startup, raised $300 million in Series C funding at a $3.4 billion valuation to develop low-cost drone and missile interceptor systems, reflecting investor appetite for asymmetric threats driven by Ukraine and Iran conflicts. The pattern suggests that 10,000 new defense companies entering the market combined with Pentagon's stated need for AI modernization creates sustained capital deployment opportunities, with established primes increasingly acting as partners rather than competitors to venture-backed firms. Yet the real constraint is not capital availability but manufacturing capacity and supply chain maturity—the Pentagon has capital but cannot deploy it faster than production bottlenecks allow, creating execution risk that venture investors must price into their underwriting.

AI-designed biologics represent an emerging dual-use technology sector with significant investment potential in therapeutics and vaccine development, yet portfolio companies face unprecedented regulatory scrutiny and biosecurity vetting that will slow commercialization timelines substantially. A Stanford University and Arc Institute research team used AI to design 16 previously unknown viruses capable of infecting bacteria, marking the first time artificial intelligence has created functional novel pathogens from scratch rather than replicating known variants. The breakthrough offers potential benefits for combating antibiotic resistance but simultaneously raises biosecurity concerns about weaponization, signaling that any frontier lab creating AI-designed biologics will face existential regulatory and reputational risk. The investment implication is that AI-designed therapeutics companies must build regulatory expertise and biosecurity frameworks as core competitive advantages—companies failing to navigate this layer will face commercialization delays and investor flight regardless of scientific merit. Similarly, critical minerals infrastructure is becoming a compelling deep-tech investment thesis driven by AI infrastructure demand, with the bottleneck in copper, rare earth elements, and specialty materials creating multi-billion dollar opportunities for geology-focused AI platforms and mining technology companies. Mariana Minerals raised $310 million in Series B funding led by Khosla Ventures with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, reflecting tier-1 VC interest in mining as an infrastructure play for AI and electrification. The startup aims to reduce metal extraction costs across copper, lithium, and other essential commodities needed to power AI infrastructure and the electrified economy.

U.S. space economy is attracting record venture capital with SpaceX planning to build robotic satellite factories on the moon and Northwood Space securing $136M in funding from government and strategic customers. SpaceX's announced plans for lunar manufacturing represent a major new capital allocation frontier, though Elon Musk's historical timeline challenges warrant investor skepticism. The critical insight is that space startups with government contracts and clear execution paths are gaining institutional traction, but technical execution risk remains existential—hardware launched to space cannot easily be recovered if systems fail, and the market will support only a limited number of viable businesses rather than a proliferation of startups. Investment selection should prioritize founders with execution track records and mission-critical applications over speculative ventures in this capital-intensive, unforgiving sector. Westinghouse and Holtec International have filed IPO paperwork with the SEC, positioning themselves as established "pure play" nuclear investments amid a U.S. reactor buildout supported by an $80 billion federal deal, potentially unlocking meaningful capital allocation opportunities in nuclear energy for the first time as established companies with real balance sheets and operational track records enter public markets.

The rebound in VC returns relative to PE is entirely driven by mega-winners, not broad portfolio performance, meaning institutional LPs should expect continued capital concentration into mega-funds that can overprice deals while emerging managers face funding drought. The investment implication: diversified exposure across sectors with proven unit economics (semiconductors, defense tech, batteries) may outperform concentrated mega-cap AI bets, and small focused funds achieving geographic arbitrage (DC at 11.7x MOIC versus Bay Area at 3.74x) present genuine return opportunities not yet reflected in mega-fund valuations.

The shift from horizontal SaaS to vertically-focused agentic AI is creating a perilous timing problem: investors must price in that competitive positioning closes within approximately one year, meaning companies like HappyRobot with 5x revenue growth and 150%+ net dollar retention in enterprise automation may command premium valuations precisely because they are solving infrastructure problems before competitors map the landscape. Yet PE investors should recognize that large, embedded enterprise platforms (Workday potentially taking private for $51B) will command premium valuations despite AI disruption, but only if they retain operational excellence. The critical investment framework shifts from revenue growth to switching cost creation and market positioning—traditional SaaS metrics have become backward-looking.

The collision between stated climate commitments and actual capital allocation toward fossil fuel infrastructure is creating a bifurcated energy market where renewable energy investors face regulatory headwinds while fossil fuel upside accelerates through 2026. Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta are openly committing billions to natural gas data center infrastructure despite climate pledges, signaling that AI compute demands are driving a near-term return to fossil fuels. Yet grid-scale battery storage is the fastest-growing energy infrastructure segment with 70% annual growth, and residential battery storage hit $11 billion in Q2 sales—an all-time high. The investment opportunity is not in choosing sides but in recognizing that companies solving material scarcity constraints (water generation, grid resilience, alternative cooling for data centers) will command premium valuations as communities recognize existential vulnerability. Water scarcity is becoming the binding constraint on data center siting, creating first-mover advantage for companies with proven generation or recycling technologies.

Defense tech is experiencing a structural shift in how capital flows to commercial ventures, with the Pentagon deploying capital at venture scale ($80M+ contracts in under 12 months through OTA mechanisms) while 10,000 new defense companies enter the market. Yet the real constraint is manufacturing capacity and supply chain maturity, not capital availability—the Pentagon has capital but cannot deploy it faster than production bottlenecks allow. This creates execution risk that venture investors must price into underwriting, and opportunity for companies solving manufacturing bottlenecks in motors, explosives, and precision components. Investors should recognize that founders with defense compliance expertise and manufacturing operational capability will command premium valuations over pure technologists, and that established primes increasingly act as partners rather than competitors to venture-backed firms.

Geopolitical competition is reshaping capital allocation across AI infrastructure, critical minerals, and space economy, with China's dominance of 90% of global rare earth processing and the U.S. responding through direct federal investment, international partnerships, and industrial policy mechanisms. Mariana Minerals' Series B success and the Trump administration's $2 billion Department of Defense commitment to battery and critical mineral production signal that mining tech is becoming a national security priority with de-risked execution timelines. SpaceX's lunar manufacturing plans and Westinghouse's IPO signal that space economy and advanced nuclear technology are attracting mainstream institutional capital. The investment implication: geopolitical tailwinds and policy support are flowing toward companies solving supply chain vulnerabilities (minerals, semiconductors, energy) rather than companies chasing TAM expansion through software innovation.

The secondary VC market is bifurcating at unprecedented speed, with recent AI startups trading at 0-5% discounts while 2021-2022 vintage companies face 54-59% discounts, signaling that older vintage legacy tech is reaching fire-sale pricing while frontier AI maintains premium valuations. Meanwhile, PE's aging asset base (40% of PE NAV now over 7 years old, up from 28.6% in 2021) is creating a distribution drought that starves reinvestment and threatens capital recycling. Buyout firms including Warburg Pincus and Leonard Green are entering the secondary PE market with dedicated GP-led deal units, leveraging sector expertise as a competitive advantage. The investment opportunity is clear: distressed software assets are reaching valuations where strategic acquirers like Bending Spoons (Airtable at $1.29B) are consolidating at steep discounts, while disciplined capital willing to wait for further compression in depressed SaaS assets will achieve superior risk-adjusted returns. The PE distribution crisis is simultaneously creating opportunity for secondaries specialists and GP-led continuation vehicles.
